title: Why I think using AI to prove the Riemann Hypothesis is important
summary:
Math is becoming increasingly difficult, and we can see that proofs are getting so complex they will probably take more than a human lifetime to solve. Don’t worry about AI stealing the joy of discovery, we still have the joy of understanding something that exists outside the human world. AI will let us tackle problems that were impossible within a single lifespan, and maybe we will even be able to understand some of the most exotic concepts. To me, AI has alien capabilities in math, just like many mathematicians and physicists do. AI's thinking feels just as alien to me as Einstein’s thinking once did. All I can do is watch these beautiful, exotic patterns unravel in front of me, and I love the idea that I get to catch a glimpse of this.

title: I Think Mathematicians and Software Engineers Will Be the Same in the Future
summary:
I now feel that the math world will eventually become like the programming world: responsible for all kinds of strange hypotheses and creations.

Then let AI verify them, do the work, get the results, and reinvent the wheel over and over again, but every wheel is made differently.

There are millions of ways to implement a feature, and the same goes for proving a mathematical conjecture.

I really miss the time before AI, the feeling of being immersed in writing code and the sense of achievement after completing a feature.

And being able to happily share with others the methods I found during development and my design ideas.

But now, I can only pursue features and rough design directions. It's become like having meetings with AI every day to discuss features.

But I can't go back to the old-fashioned way of programming anymore, because I can no longer purely immerse myself in writing a program.

Because I know that whatever I write, AI can do it in a few seconds, and do it better. I can't get any sense of achievement, and the time I spend becomes purely a waste of time.

I've already given up now. I'm not some top student from a top university, or some top talent who has worked at a top company.

The ambition I used to have is gone. All that's left is the thought of "destroy everything together, then create completely new rules and a new world."

title: Ask HN: CVE craziness – are you on a path to burnout?
summary:
With AI stripmining every code publicly accessible, CVE rates soaring, and maintainers under pressure, are they on their way to a burnout?

I've seen some commenters going like "just the usual stream of CVEs & fixes, business as usual". We know that's not true.

The past few weeks were exciting. PHP, eMudhra, widespread attacks on supermarket fridges, full-day+ outage of MSFT cloud systems & more. If this were a blip, okay. But some experts estimate this could be the new 'normal' for a year, 2 years or longer (until most bugs have been shaken out). Which made me think of the human aspect.

Are you maintainer of a software project affected by this? Making extra hours? Losing sleep? Is a burnout in the stars? Would that be something you could feel coming? Any way to mitigate this?

Asking because, well... if this keeps going, maintainers burn out, patching/mitigation work suffer, and obviously that would affect the public at large not just professionals.

Maybe AI can help here as well. But regardless: maintainers' lives matter (MLM).

title: Ask HN: Are startups today worth it even in a best case scenario?
summary:
I'm gonna open this with the disclaimer that this is purely a financial and risk comparison post. No one is complaining that we are poorly compensated. It is good to discuss compensation so we can make informed and educated decisions when deciding how to commit the next few years of our lives.

A close friend of mine joined an AI startup (being intentionally vague) around 1.5 years ago and despite the company doing extremely well on valuation, I'm surprised at how he's not really better off than just working at a large tech company.

Concrete numbers for the startup: -200k salary -Equity grant over 4 years is 500k -The company's valuation has since went from single billions to tens of billions, leaving him with a 10x multiplier when looking only at valuation. After you account for dilution, it's closer to 6x. -Liquidity event annually allows you to sell 10% of your vested shares

Big tech at a similar years of experience is around 400-500k total comp, and the RSU component is generally liquid.

For example sake and ease of calculation, if you assume that my friend's entire equity was vested, and he was able to sell 10% of it, it would amount to approximately $300k/liquidity event, which brings him to around 500k a year as well (200k + 300k). In reality, he's really only able to access $300k/4 since that's all he has vested and that brings him closer to $75k for this liquidity event. There are a lot of variables I'm leaving out obviously such as potential future value, IPO, etc., but the thing that is surprising to me overall is that this is a close to best case outcome, yet the employee doesn't really end up any better off than big tech due to lack of liquidity and dilution. I mean I get it, impact, interesting work, etc. -- the qualitative measures -- aren't really accounted for, but I'm not looking to make a wholistic comparison.

This brings me to the question: Is the risk in a startup ever justified for a lower level employee (engineer, Product Manager, Program Manager, etc.)?

title: Ask HN: Could AI's RH proof have used human work found in its training data?
summary:
When reading of third-party validations of AI's RH proof [0] that:

> While still possible, the proof exploiting a bug is vanishingly small now.

it makes me think we're realising in real-time that we're living through the most important time in human history. Moreso than during the invention of computers, the internet, or the wheel.

Problem: many people worked on RH, and some would have stored their attempts at proofs in places like GitHub or google docs - places that may have been ended up in training datasets.

Therefore, is it possible that Claude knew some significant parts of the proof (potentially even all of it but scattered across multiple private sources) and it merely assembled the parts into a single proof, as opposed to having thought of the proof for itself? [1]

(The distinction matters because assembling parts of existing proofs seems different to authoring a proof by oneself.)

[0] https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50590943

[1] I recall AI did something similar with an early Ergos problem (although it used public works), where it found connections and technically solved some unsolved problem, but Terence Tao came out a few days later saying it connected dots but didn't really think of anything truely novel.
